title: Limits, scanning and reproducible builds
summary: Cap memory and CPU, read exit code 137, scan images for CVEs, and make builds repeatable.

steps.title: Resource limits
body: Without limits, one leaking container can starve every other on the host. cgroups let you cap it:
- If the process exceeds `--memory`, the kernel's **OOM killer** kills it: the container exits with **137** (128 + SIGKILL 9) and `docker inspect` shows `"OOMKilled": true`.
- .NET and modern Node respect container limits: the .NET GC sizes its heap from the cgroup memory limit, and `Environment.ProcessorCount` reflects `--cpus`.
`docker stats` shows live usage against the limits.

steps.prompt: The API keeps dying with `Exited (137)` under load. `docker inspect` shows `"OOMKilled": true` and `--memory 256m`. What is happening?
options: The process used more than 256 MB and the kernel killed it; raise the limit or reduce memory use
Docker stopped it gracefully with SIGTERM
steps.explain: 137 without OOMKilled usually means someone ran `docker kill`, or a stop timed out.

steps.prompt: Match each flag to its effect.
pairs: hard memory cap; exceeding it gets the process OOM-killed
at most one and a half CPU cores of time; throttles, never kills
caps the number of processes, stopping fork bombs
makes the container's root filesystem read-only
restart the container when it exits, unless you stopped it

steps.title: Scanning and reproducible builds
body: **Scanning.** Tools like `docker scout cves`, Trivy and Grype list known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in an image's OS packages and app dependencies. Most findings come from the **base image**, so the usual fix is *rebuild on an updated base*, not patch by hand. Scan in CI and fail the build only on serious findings that have a fix available, otherwise the noise teaches people to ignore it. Rebuild regularly even without code changes, to pick up base-image patches.
**Reproducibility.** The same commit should produce the same image:
- pin base images by tag, or better by digest (`FROM node:22.11-alpine@sha256:...`);
- install from lock files (`npm ci`, `dotnet restore --locked-mode`, `pip install -r` with pinned versions);
- keep `.dockerignore` tight so stray local files cannot change the build.

steps.prompt: Does it make builds more **reproducible** or less?
items: `npm ci` with a committed lock file

steps.prompt: The scanner reports a CRITICAL CVE in `openssl` that comes from the base image `debian:trixie-slim`, and a fixed version exists. What is the right response?
options: Rebuild with `--pull` (or bump the pinned base digest) so the image picks up the patched base, then redeploy
Ignore it: base image findings are not your problem
Switch the app to HTTP so OpenSSL is not used
steps.explain: Base images are patched constantly; your job is to rebuild on them. A scheduled weekly rebuild keeps this from piling up.

steps.prompt: The container was killed for using too much memory. What does this print?

steps.title: Put limits on a running container
prompt: This terminal has a **real Docker Engine**. The container `batch` runs with **no limits**: one runaway job can take
the whole host's memory and CPU from `api`. See it: `docker stats --no-stream`.
Without recreating `batch` (it is in the middle of a run), limit it to:
1. **128 MB** of memory, with no extra swap;
3. and make Docker restart it if it crashes, at most 3 times.

checks.name: memory is 128 MB with no extra swap
checks.fail: `batch` should have `--memory 128m --memory-swap 128m` (swap equal to memory means no extra swap).

checks.name: half a CPU
checks.fail: `batch` is not limited to half a CPU: `--cpus 0.5`.

checks.name: restart on failure, at most 3 times
it is the same container, still running
checks.fail: `batch` was recreated or stopped. `docker update` changes limits on a running container. Press Reset scenario.

hints: `docker update` changes the resource limits and restart policy of an existing container, without a restart.
`--memory 128m --memory-swap 128m` (when you set `--memory` on a container that has swap, set `--memory-swap` too).
steps.explain: Limits are cgroup settings, so they can change while the process runs: `docker update` is the on-call fix for a noisy neighbour, and the same numbers go into `docker run` or Compose (`mem_limit`, `cpus`, or `deploy.resources`) for next time. Without a memory limit a leak takes the whole host; with one, the kernel kills just that container (exit 137, `OOMKilled: true`).

steps.title: Gate the build on a scan report
prompt: This terminal is a real Linux machine with `jq`. Your CI scans every image with Trivy
(`trivy image --format json -o report.json IMAGE`); last night's reports are in `~/ci/reports/`. Look at one:
Write `~/ci/gate.sh REPORT` so that it prints one line per finding that is **HIGH or CRITICAL and has a fix**, in report
order, as `ID: upgrade PACKAGE to FIXED`, and **exits 1** when there is any such line, **0** otherwise.

checks.name: api.json: two blocking findings, exit 1
checks.fail: For `api.json` the gate should print the two fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings and exit 1.

checks.name: web.json: nothing fixable, exit 0
checks.fail: For `web.json` the only CRITICAL has no fix and the fixable one is MEDIUM: print nothing and exit 0.

checks.name: a report with no findings passes
checks.fail: A clean report (Trivy writes no `Vulnerabilities` key, or null) should print nothing and exit 0.

hints: The filter: `(.Severity == "HIGH" or .Severity == "CRITICAL") and .FixedVersion != null`. The `[]?` copes with a missing list.
Save the lines in a variable, print them, and `[ -z "$out" ]` decides the exit code.
solution: # Usage: gate.sh REPORT.json  - fail the build on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings.
steps.explain: This is the usual CI policy: block on what you can fix today, track the rest. Trivy can do the simple version itself (`trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 IMAGE`), but teams often post-process the JSON like this to add exceptions, comment on pull requests or feed a dashboard. Unfixable criticals still matter: they go on a list with an owner and a review date.
